To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
moral decision making is an unconscious, automatic, and rapid process that is influenced by a number of factors.

(1) moral decision making is not a rational process; (2) moral decisions are not always made consciously; (3) moral decision making involves the interaction of multiple cognitive systems, each of which evolved for different purposes; and (4) moral decision making depends on the interaction of multiple neural networks, each of which has its own unique neuroanatomical and neurochemical characteristics.

moral decision making is a process of intuitive moral judgment and deliberation, that the process is influenced by the context, that it is influenced by the individual's personality and that it is influenced, to a large extent, by the moral intuitions that the individual has acquired through social learning.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the moral decision making process works and the factors that influence it.
how moral decisions are made and the factors that influence them.
the development of moral competence.

there is no single theory of ethics that is applicable to all professions, and there are no single set of ethical standards or principles that are universally applicable across all professions.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the research findings indicate that moral decisions are made in the brain, that the brain is a moral agent, and that moral decisions are based on a complex interaction between cognitive and affective processes.
the research findings indicate that the moral behavior of psychologists is not only a function of their cognitive abilities, but also their emotional and motivational states.
the psychology profession has not taken advantage of the vast amount of research data that is relevant to the development of ethics courses.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the psychology profession has an opportunity to enhance pre practicum training in professional ethics by integrating the findings of contemporary psychological and neuroscience research into ethics training programs.
the research findings suggest that educators should not focus on the cognitive aspects of moral decision making to the exclusion of affect and emotion.

educators who teach ethics should consider the following points when developing their courses: (1) the importance of the moral emotions; (2) the importance of empathy and perspective taking; (3) the importance of moral identity; (4) the importance of self-regulation; (5) the importance of social context; (6) the importance of cognitive biases; (7) the importance of intuition; and (8) the importance of motivation.
